question: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is inherited as an X-linked recessive condition, so it almost exclusively affects males, while females are typically carriers.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is true. DMD follows X-linked recessive inheritance. The DMD gene is on chromosome Xp21 and encodes the cytoskeletal protein dystrophin. Because males have only one X chromosome, a single mutated copy leads to absent dystrophin and the full disease. Females with one mutated and one normal copy are typically carriers — they may have mildly elevated CK but rarely develop significant weakness. This inheritance pattern explains why affected males cluster in the maternal side of the family.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. DMD is caused by out-of-frame mutations in the DMD gene on chromosome Xp21, resulting in absent dystrophin protein. It is X-linked recessive: affected males (XY) have only one copy of the gene and cannot compensate; carrier females (XX) usually have one normal allele and are clinically unaffected, though some carriers have mildly elevated CK and rarely symptoms. The maternal uncle described in clinical scenarios (affected through the mother's carrier X chromosome) is a classic X-linked pedigree.
